rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient at mid temperature to elute all 10 compounds if possible and map the overall retention window and any hold-eluting peaks. This gives a balanced first read on where to narrow the phi window and whether slope or temperature will be the better lever next.

All compounds are already baseline resolved, so the only score to gain is by pulling the last peak earlier while keeping resolution above 1.5. The first and last peaks correspond to roughly phi_e about 0.11 and 0.59, so trimming the gradient window to that elution window should keep all peaks in-gradient and shorten the run substantially without making the slope excessively steep.

Narrowing the phi window made everything later, so the main lever for a better CRF is likely temperature. Increase T to 60 C while returning to the successful broad gradient to shorten retention and check whether the closest midrun pair stays resolved or even improves via a small selectivity shift.

At 60 C the run is fully resolved and already close to the 10 min target, so the best chance is a modestly steeper version of the successful method to pull the last peak under 10 min while staying above R=1.5 for the closest pair. A small change in tG is safer than changing the phi window because the broad window has behaved well and the limiting pair is only moderately close.

The current method is nearly optimal, but the limiting factor is the 4/5 pair just below full credit; a small temperature decrease may restore selectivity for that pair while only modestly lengthening the run. Because 60 C strongly accelerated the method and changing tG from 20 to 18 mainly hurt that pair, temperature is the cleanest lever to try next.

We are very close to the optimum and need to see whether a slightly steeper gradient can push the last peak below 10 min enough to offset any small further loss in the weakest pair. The 4/5 pair worsened when going from 20 to 18 min, so this is a controlled boundary test around the current best point.

Keep the near-optimal 18 min, 60 C conditions but slightly lower phi1 to make the late part of the gradient shallower, aiming to improve the borderline 4/5 pair without greatly delaying the last peak. The last compound should still remain in-gradient, since under the 0.95 method it eluted at an estimated phi_e well below 0.90.

The key tradeoff is temperature-dependent selectivity: at 60 C the 4/5 pair is limiting, while at 55 C the weak pair shifted to 6/7, so probing 50 C can reveal whether a more favorable selectivity window exists that gives all pairs at or above 1.5 with only a small time penalty. This is the most promising remaining orthogonal lever around the current optimum.

At 18 min, lowering phi1 from 0.95 to 0.90 restored full credit for the critical 4/5 pair but made the run slightly too long; at 16 min with phi1 0.95 the run is fast enough but 4/5 is under-resolved. Combining the faster tG with the slightly lower phi1 is the best targeted attempt to keep t_last near or below 10 min while lifting that limiting pair back toward full resolution.

We know lowering phi1 to 0.90 at 18 min fixed the borderline 4/5 pair but made the run a bit too long; a further small reduction in phi1 tests whether selectivity for that pair improves enough to outweigh the extra retention. This refines the phi1 trend at the current best tG and temperature without changing multiple factors at once.

Temperature has a strong and non-monotonic effect on which pair is limiting, so testing the untried combination adjacent to the fully resolved 20 min, 60 C run may reveal a sweet spot where all pairs remain at full credit and the last peak lands close to 10 min. This is a focused check of the only nearby condition space that could plausibly beat the current best by improving selectivity without over-compressing the gradient.

The temperature trend suggests a selectivity crossover: 60 C favors the 6/7 pair but hurts 4/5, while 55 C and 50 C strongly hurt 6/7. Running 20 min at 50 C isolates whether the gentler slope can rescue 6/7 enough to reveal a useful alternative selectivity regime, since 18 min at 50 C was too compressed.

At 20 min and 60 C all pairs were fully resolved but the last peak was slightly late; lowering phi1 to 0.90 may shift selectivity favorably while keeping the critical 4/5 pair comfortably above 1.5. This tests whether the broader 20 min slope can tolerate a slightly shallower upper-end window better than the 18 min run did.

The temperature dependence is highly non-monotonic, with the limiting pair switching between 4/5 and 6/7, so there is still a chance of a narrow selectivity sweet spot between 50 and 55 C. Testing 45 C at the near-optimal 18 min condition is a targeted check for a crossover that could restore all pair credits without much extra run time.

The remaining untested possibility is a strong temperature-selectivity crossover below 40 C, since 40 C was fully resolved at a longer gradient and the identity of the limiting pair changes with temperature. A low-temperature probe at the near-optimal 18 min gradient checks whether all pairs can stay resolved while the late peak remains close enough to 10 min to compete.

A final temperature probe between the benign 40 C run and the poor low-temperature region checks for any narrow selectivity optimum that could still surpass the current best. This isolates the only substantially untested neighborhood where the limiting pair might improve without changing the already near-optimal gradient geometry.

The results strongly indicate 60 C is optimal and the decisive tradeoff is only between last-peak time and the 4/5 resolution around tG 18–20 min. A 22 min run will map the local slope–resolution response of that pair more clearly and bound whether the gain in its resolution is close to linear, helping confirm that injection 4 is truly the practical optimum.

We have explored tG, phi1, and temperature extensively, but not the effect of a slightly higher starting composition around the best condition. Raising phi0 may reduce dead time spent on very early peaks and subtly reshape the early-to-mid gradient occupancy, which could improve the 4/5 pair without the larger late-peak penalty seen when lowering phi1.

Among fast methods, lowering phi1 improved the limiting 4/5 pair at 18 min, and the 16 min, 0.90 run was already close to the best score. Pushing phi1 one step lower at 16 min tests whether extra selectivity gain for 4/5 can outweigh the expected modest delay of the last peak while still keeping t_last near 10 min.

This interpolates between the fast but slightly under-resolved 16 min, 0.90 method and the fully resolved but slower 16 min, 0.80 method. It is the cleanest remaining shot at achieving full pair credit with a last peak close enough to 10 min to challenge the current best.

Injection 20 exactly matches the retention pattern and score of injection 4, showing a ridge of equivalent conditions where only the effective slope matters. Testing 18 min with phi1 0.80 checks whether moving further along that ridge can finally lift the 4/5 pair above 1.5 while keeping the last peak close enough to 10 min to improve CRF.

We have bracketed a tradeoff ridge at 16 min where lower phi1 improves the 4/5 pair but delays the last peak. Testing 0.75 is the last focused interpolation on that ridge to see whether a slightly stronger selectivity gain can produce a net CRF gain over the current tie for best.

The best region is clearly at 60 C, and the unresolved issue is whether a slightly steeper gradient can still keep enough 4/5 selectivity if the upper phi window is lowered. This probes the remaining fast-side corner near the optimum where t_last may stay under 10 min and the 4/5 pair could land closer to the 1.5 threshold than the 16 min runs.

At 14 min and 0.90, the run is fast enough but the 4/5 pair is too compressed; lowering phi1 by one step is the best remaining way to recover selectivity for that pair while likely keeping t_last under 10 min. This targets the same favorable fast regime that produced the best scores, but with a slightly shallower late gradient.

One last targeted shot is to continue lowering phi1 in the fast 14 min regime, where t_last is already safely below 10 min and the only deficit is the 4/5 pair. If that pair gains enough selectivity from the shallower late gradient, this could beat the current best despite some increase in retention of the last peak.
